title: The First Images
description: Lascaux, Chauvet, the Neanderthal question and the so-called Venus figurines

concepts.title: Into the Dark: Lascaux and Chauvet
concepts.contentHtml:
Art history asks simple questions about made things: what is it, how was it made, who made it, and what did it mean to the people who first saw it? Some of the oldest answers lie underground. On 12 September 1940 four boys examined the foxhole down which their dog had fallen on the hill of Lascaux, in the Dordogne region of south-western France.1 By the light of a makeshift lamp, they found walls covered in animals.

Lascaux holds close to 600 paintings and around 1,400 engravings, dated to about 17,000 to 15,000 BCE. Horses are the most numerous, followed by deer and aurochs, a now-extinct wild cattle. The entrance leads straight into the Hall of the Bulls, where four large bulls tower above fleeing horses and deer, drawn in side view but with their horns turned. Red came from hematite and black from charcoal or manganese oxides, applied with fingers, charcoal, brushes of hair or moss, or blown through a hollow bone. Here is a puzzle: the nearest known source of Lascaux's particular manganese oxides is some 250 kilometres away, in the central Pyrenees.2

Chauvet, above the river Ardèche near the Pont-d'Arc, was found on 18 December 1994 by Jean-Marie Chauvet, Éliette Brunel and Christian Hillaire. You met its dates in the Prehistory topic; it is far older than Lascaux. Most of its more than 420 animal images show creatures people did not hunt, such as lions, rhinoceroses and bears. In the Panel of the Lions, a pride of 16 lions chases seven bison across a wall that was scraped clean first, with shading smudged in by hand3 (stump-drawing). Nearby, two rhinoceroses stand face to face, horns crossed, just as males fight in the wild.

One popular picture is misleading: the painted caves were not everyday homes. Lascaux shows only temporary occupation, probably linked to making the art. The cave closed to the public in 1963 after crowds of visitors caused algae to grow on its walls, and Chauvet has been sealed from the start. Visitors see replicas instead, such as Lascaux II, opened in 1983.

concepts.title: Did Neanderthals Paint First?
concepts.contentHtml:
Researchers often date something touching a painting rather than the paint itself. One method is uranium-thorium (U-Th) dating. Water seeping over a cave wall can leave thin crusts of carbonate on top of the paint. These crusts contain traces of uranium, which decays to thorium at a steady rate, so the ratio of the two tells you when the crust formed. Because the crust grew after the paint, its age is a minimum age for whatever lies beneath.

In February 2018 a team from the University of Southampton and the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology, with Dirk Hoffmann as joint lead author, published U-Th results in Science from more than 60 carbonate samples in three Spanish caves 700 kilometres apart: La Pasiega, Maltravieso and Ardales. The caves hold red and black signs, dots, hand stencils and engravings, and some marks came out older than 64,000 years. That is about 20,000 years before modern humans reached Europe, so the team argued the painters must have been Neanderthals, Europe's only humans at the time.1

The claim drew fire. Some critics doubted that Neanderthals had the mental capacity for such work; a sharper objection, reported in 2019, was about chemistry. If water running over a crust had washed out some of its uranium, the crust would look older than it is, and the paintings could be tens of thousands of years younger, well within the time of modern humans.2 Others suggested that some red stains might simply be natural.

In 2021 a team led by Africa Pitarch Martí and João Zilhão tested that last idea at Ardales, where red paint covers curtains of stalagmite. Using microscopy, X-ray diffraction and Raman spectroscopy, they confirmed the marks were human-made, and they showed the pigment did not come from the iron-rich deposits known inside the cave.3 Its make-up is consistent with people returning to paint there more than once; dates from the panel range from more than 45,900 to more than 65,500 years. The debate is not closed, but the question of who counts as an artist is now argued with laboratory data.

concepts.title: The So-Called Venus Figurines
concepts.contentHtml:
Not all Ice Age art is on walls. More than 200 small statuettes of women have been found at Upper Palaeolithic sites across Europe and as far afield as Siberia, made by people separated by up to 30,000 years. Most are between 2.5 and 10.2 centimetres tall, and the commonest material is mammoth tusk. Many share a recipe: large breasts, hips and belly, with the face, arms and feet left vague or missing.

The most famous is the Venus of Willendorf, found on 7 August 1908 on the left bank of the Danube at Willendorf in Lower Austria and now in the Natural History Museum in Vienna. She is exactly 110 millimetres tall: faceless, with heavy breasts, a protruding belly and a carefully worked headdress or hairstyle covering her head.1 She was carved from oolitic limestone, a stone built of tiny grains called ooids, and painted red, possibly with ochre, though cleaning at the time of discovery removed almost all of it. She is roughly 30,000 years old.

Then came a surprise. In 2022 Gerhard Weber and colleagues published micro-CT scans of her interior in Scientific Reports. Comparing her grains with oolite samples from France to Ukraine, they found the closest match at Sega di Ala, near Lake Garda in northern Italy, with a site in eastern Ukraine as a less likely second.2 Either the figure or its stone crossed the Alps, perhaps over years or even generations.

The oldest known example, the Venus of Hohle Fels from a cave at Schelklingen in Germany, is carved from woolly mammoth ivory and is between 35,000 and 40,000 years old. Instead of a head it has a loop, so it may have been worn as a pendant. And the name? It is a modern label: these figures are thousands of years older than any myth of the Roman goddess Venus, and archaeologists usually say the word with air quotes.3 Fertility symbols, mother goddesses, amulets for childbirth, dolls and ideals of beauty have all been proposed, and the evidence settles none of them. Remember, too, that animals, not women, dominate Ice Age art.

title: Egypt, Greece and Rome: Bodies by the Rules
description: Egypt's grid, the Greek kouros and canon, painted marble and Roman copies

concepts.title: Egypt: A Grid for Eternity
concepts.contentHtml:
Ancient Egyptian art was made to work, not just to please. Tomb paintings and temple reliefs served the dead and the gods, so they were meant to last forever. That is why faces look calm: emotions are fleeting, and an eternal image should show a whole existence rather than one passing mood.

Look up the Narmer Palette (about 3150 BCE), a ceremonial slab of siltstone a little over 64 centimetres tall, found in 1897–98 at Nekhen (Hierakonpolis). It celebrates King Narmer. His body follows a rule you will meet throughout Egyptian art, the composite view: the head is in profile, yet the eye is drawn frontally, as if you were face to face;1 the shoulders are frontal, while the torso, legs and feet are in profile. It is a code, not clumsiness.

The code came with a measuring system. An artist drew a small version of a scene, ruled grid lines on it, drew the same grid on the plastered wall and copied it square by square. Grids of squares survive from Dynasty 11 onwards, often where a finished layer of paint has fallen off. A standing figure filled 18 squares from the soles of the feet to the hairline: the knee fell on line 6, the elbow on line 12 and the junction of neck and shoulders on line 16.2 By Dynasty 25 artists were using a grid of 21 squares instead. Whatever the size of the wall, the figure kept its proportions.

The great exception is the reign of Akhenaten at Amarna, when art turned more realistic. The bust of Nefertiti, his queen, was found there in 1912 by the German archaeologist Ludwig Borchardt, in the workshop of the sculptor Thutmose. It is limestone covered with modelled gypsum, still brightly painted, with one eye inlaid in crystal and a pupil of black wax. Only one eye? The second inlay was never made, because the bust was a workshop model never meant for display.3 It is now in the Egyptian Museum (Neues Museum) in Berlin, and Egypt disputes the way it left the country.

concepts.title: Greece: From Kouros to Canon
concepts.contentHtml:
Greek sculptors learned from Egypt. The earliest large Greek stone figures, the kouroi (nude young men) and korai (clothed young women), are as rigid as Egyptian statues, with arms held straight at the sides and eyes staring blankly ahead. A good one to look up is the New York Kouros of about 590–580 BCE, carved in marble from the island of Naxos, 194.6 centimetres tall and now in the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York.

Over the next century the stone loosens. By around 480 BCE the last kouroi carry their weight on one leg; the other hip drops, the buttocks and shoulders relax, the head is less stiff and a hint of a smile appears.1 Art historians call this shift of weight contrapposto ("counterpose"), and it makes a figure look poised to move.

The sculptor Polykleitos turned the new body into theory. Besides statues such as the Doryphoros (Spear-bearer), he wrote a treatise, the Kanon, on the techniques of sculpture, stressing correct proportion. Many of the most admired Greek statues reach you only through later copies. Rome loved Greek sculpture so much that, once the supply of originals ran out, sculptors made copies;2 Rome itself had a school for copying Greek masterpieces, headed by Pasiteles and active in the 1st century BCE. Copies are evidence with flaws: they lack the master's touch, may swap bronze for marble and can even mix up heads.

Originals in bronze are rarer still. One count puts the surviving examples of Greek bronze sculpture at no more than twelve, and some of the finest were saved by the sea, a better keeper of bronzes than people have been: the two Riace Warriors (460–450 BCE) are among them. Here is a surprise: the dark green surface those bronzes have today is not what the Greeks wanted. Sanctuaries employed cleaners and polishers to keep statues a shiny reddish-brass colour.3

concepts.title: The Myth of White Marble
concepts.contentHtml:
For Renaissance artists, ancient sculpture meant gleaming white marble, and their admiration shaped Western taste for centuries. But the sculpture and architecture of the ancient world were brightly and elaborately painted. They look white to us because centuries of weathering wore most of the paint away, and cleaning by later collectors probably removed more.1 By classical standards, the bare surface of Michelangelo's David would have looked unfinished. Scholars were arguing for painted sculpture as early as 1815, yet the white ideal proved hard to shift.

The German archaeologists Vinzenz Brinkmann and Ulrike Koch-Brinkmann spent more than two decades gathering the evidence; Brinkmann was taking ultraviolet photographs in the museums of Athens in 1982. Their toolkit, which you will meet again in this subject, includes:

  • Raking light, shone low across the surface, to reveal incised details and the patterns left as different paints weathered unevenly.
  • Ultraviolet light, to bring out slight surface differences where paint once was.
  • X-ray fluorescence and infrared spectroscopy, to identify the pigments.

Their best-known case is a life-size Trojan archer from the west pediment of the Temple of Aphaia on the island of Aegina, now in the Glyptothek in Munich. The figure wears a shirt and leggings covered with an intricate red, yellow, blue and green diamond pattern, a bright yellow vest with lions and griffins and a tall yellow hat, all revealed under UV light on the faded original.2 He probably represents Paris, and the Greeks often showed Trojans like Persians, exotic and overdressed beside largely naked Greek heroes.

The colour still shocks. When a German newspaper printed the archer's reconstruction in 2001, in black and white, readers were indignant at the vivid colours.3 Some caution is due: scholars do not know whether paint went on in one coat or two, how finely it was ground or which binder was used, so a reconstruction is a model. Roman marble was painted too, while Roman private portrait busts showed sitters old, wrinkled and scarred, a realism that may come from wax funeral masks of ancestors kept at home.

title: The Middle Ages: Icons, Books and Light
description: Byzantine icons and iconoclasm, the Book of Kells, and the Gothic cathedral's new light

concepts.title: Icons and the War on Images
concepts.contentHtml:
In the Byzantine Empire, the Christian empire ruled from Constantinople, an icon could be any image of a holy figure, but the word usually means a small portable painting on a wooden panel. Many were made with encaustic: coloured pigments mixed with wax and burned into the wood. Icons were not decoration. People prayed and bowed to them, kissed them, and lit incense and tapers before them. Icons were produced from the 3rd century and became popular from the 6th.

The place to find the earliest survivors is the Holy Monastery of Saint Catherine at Sinai, which has several icons from the 6th century. Among them is a magnificent Pantokrator ("All-Ruler"), probably donated by the emperor Justinian I (r. 527–565) to mark the monastery's foundation.1 The Pantokrator became the standard image of Christ: seen full frontal, holding a Gospel book in his left hand and blessing with his right, looking straight back at you.

Then came iconoclasm, literally "the destruction of images", which peaked in two waves, 726–787 and 814–843. Its theologians argued that images reopened old disputes about how Christ could be both human and divine. In 730 the emperor Leo III formally decreed that all icons must be destroyed, and Pope Gregory III answered that anyone guilty of such destruction would be excommunicated.2 Leo destroyed the largest icon in Constantinople, the golden Christ above his own palace gates. Huge numbers of icons were destroyed or defaced, and many wall paintings were repainted with simple crosses, the only symbol the iconoclasts allowed.

The fight ended in 843, when the regent Theodora had the veneration of icons proclaimed Orthodox. Eastern Christians still celebrate the moment as the Triumph of Orthodoxy on the first Sunday of Lent. For art history, the lesson is blunt: whole categories of images can vanish in a generation, which is why the Sinai panels are so precious.

concepts.title: The Book of Kells: Painting on Skin
concepts.contentHtml:
Before printing, every book was written by hand, and the grandest were illuminated manuscripts, their pages lit up with colour and gold. The most famous is the Book of Kells (about 800), the four Gospels in Latin, 33 by 25 centimetres, written on vellum, prepared animal skin. Portraits of the Evangelists and pages of lettering are framed with intricate Celtic knotwork, and the letters of the Chi-Rho page, the monogram of Christ, have been called more living presences than letters. Around 1185 the writer Gerald of Wales (Giraldus Cambrensis), probably describing this book, called it "the work of an angel, not of a man".

Making such a book took a team. Monks raised the animals, turned their skins into vellum, cut sheets to size and ruled lines, leaving spaces for pictures. A scribe wrote the text, a second monk added titles in blue or red, and an illuminator sketched the images, laying gold first and colours after. Kells was written by three anonymous scribes known today as Hand A, Hand B and Hand C.1 Wait, really? A painting in a manuscript is called a miniature, but not because it is small. The word comes from Latin miniare, "to colour in red", after minium, the red pigment cinnabar used for the initials of early books.

Where it was made is disputed. Monks of St Columba's order on Iona, an island off Scotland, probably began it there and took it to Kells in Ireland after Viking raids; a raid in 806 killed 68 monks at Iona.2 In 1007 thieves stole it from the abbey and tore off its cover of gold and jewels, and the text itself was found discarded. During Oliver Cromwell's invasion of Ireland it was sent to Dublin for safe keeping, and in 1661 Bishop Henry Jones gave it to Trinity College Dublin, where it is still on show. Its pages are turned several times a year to protect them. In 2011 the town of Kells asked for a volume back, and Trinity refused.3

concepts.title: Gothic: Architecture Made of Light
concepts.contentHtml:
Romanesque churches had thick, heavy walls and rounded arches. In the 12th century a new style began just north of Paris. Abbot Suger (1081–1151), abbot of Saint-Denis from 1122 and for a time regent of France, rebuilt his abbey church between 1137 and 1148, creating what became the archetype of the Gothic cathedral.1 For Suger, light itself was divine: beautiful, luminous things could lift the mind from the earthly realm towards heaven, so he wanted his church flooded with light.

To get that light, builders combined three devices:

  • Pointed arches, which bear weight better than round ones and point towards heaven.
  • Rib vaults, a diagonal stone framework you can see criss-crossing the ceiling.
  • Flying buttresses, external props that push back against the outward thrust of the walls.

Together they let walls rise taller and thinner, opening them to huge stained-glass windows held in stone tracery, including great circular rose windows. Suger's west front at Saint-Denis, with three portals and a rose window, set a pattern that spread across Europe. For the full effect, visit Chartres Cathedral, south-west of Paris, built around 1190 to 1220. Its 167 stained-glass windows make up perhaps the most impressive surviving collection of medieval glass.

Here is the twist: no medieval builder called this style Gothic. The name came from Giorgio Vasari (1511–1574), the Italian artist and writer whose works are often treated as the basis of modern art history. Writing after the style had fallen out of favour, he meant the label as an insult, linking the buildings to the "barbaric" Goths who had invaded Rome over a thousand years earlier.2 The name stuck, but the verdict did not: a Gothic revival began in the late 18th century.

title: The Renaissance: Weight, Space and Oil
description: Giotto, Brunelleschi's perspective, van Eyck's oil, and the myths of Leonardo and Michelangelo

concepts.title: Giotto and Brunelleschi: Weight and Space
concepts.contentHtml:
Medieval religious images were often flat and formulaic, figures to pray to rather than people to believe in. Giotto di Bondone (born 1267 or 1277, died 1337) changed that. His masterpiece is the cycle of frescoes in the Scrovegni Chapel, also called the Arena Chapel, in Padua, worked on from about 1304 for Enrico Scrovegni, a rich banker whose moneylending father appears in Dante's Inferno. Thirty-eight scenes from the lives of the Virgin Mary and Christ run in three rows around the walls,1 each side panel about 2 by 1.85 metres, many set against a deep blue that matches the starry ceiling.

Giotto used highlights and shadows to make bodies look round and solid, painted buildings in three dimensions and gave faces real emotion. In his Last Supper, five apostles sit with their backs to you, so you look over their heads. In the Kiss of Judas, Judas's brilliant yellow cloak almost swallows Christ as the two stand nose to nose.

A century later, Florence added mathematics. The goldsmith turned architect Filippo Brunelleschi (1377–1446) pioneered linear perspective: creating the illusion of depth on a flat surface by making imaginary sightlines converge on a central point. In the mid-1420s he demonstrated it in public on the steps of Florence's cathedral, using mirrors, a pinhole and two paintings (now lost) of the Baptistery and the city, insisting on a single point of view.2 In 1435 Leon Battista Alberti set out the method in his treatise De pictura (On Painting), advising that the single vanishing point should be at the viewer's eye level.3

Brunelleschi also built what most architects thought impossible, the dome of Florence Cathedral. Completed in 1436, it is 45.5 metres across and 91 metres high, made of bricks in a herringbone pattern with a double shell, and it was raised without fixed wooden centring to hold it up during construction.

concepts.title: Van Eyck and the Oil Myth
concepts.contentHtml:
Now go north to the Low Countries and look up the Arnolfini Portrait by Jan van Eyck, signed and dated 1434, in the National Gallery in London. It is only 82 by 60 centimetres, painted in oil on an oak panel. A richly dressed couple, probably the Italian merchant Giovanni di Nicolao di Arnolfini and his wife, stand in a room in Bruges. He wears a hat of plaited straw and a dark fur-trimmed tabard and raises his hand; she wears a green wool dress trimmed with white fur. Above them hangs a brass chandelier with one lit candle, and on the back wall a convex mirror reflects two men at the door, beneath a Latin inscription: "Jan van Eyck was here. 1434".

Two popular beliefs about this picture are wrong. She is not pregnant: she is holding up her bulky, fashionable gown, as ladies commonly did.1 And it is no longer read as a wedding ceremony. Even the room is invented: the chandelier could not fit the space and there is no fireplace.

The biggest myth is that van Eyck invented oil painting. A note sent with this very picture to the Prince Regent in 1816 still called him "the person who first discovered the art of Painting in Oil Colours". He did not. In 2008 scientists at the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility showed that 12 of the 50 caves at Bamiyan in Afghanistan had murals painted in oil in the mid-7th century.2 What van Eyck mastered was a technique: building paint up in translucent layers, or glazes, for minutely realistic surfaces and natural light. The National Gallery notes that nothing in his pigments is unusual; the illusion relied on skill.3 He worked fast, even with his fingers, and left a thumbprint by the shadow of the dog's leg.

How do we know about the making? Infrared reflectography, which sees through paint to the drawing beneath, shows the underdrawing was done in stages. At first van Eyck left out the terrier, the chandelier, the chair, the beads and the shoes, painting them in late, and he altered both faces.

concepts.title: Leonardo and Michelangelo: Legends and Facts
concepts.contentHtml:
By 1500 Italian painters had perspective, oil and anatomy, and two of them became legends. Leonardo da Vinci's Mona Lisa shows Lisa Gherardini, wife of the Florentine silk merchant Francesco del Giocondo, against a distant landscape, turning towards you with her famous smile. It is painted not on canvas but on a panel of poplar wood, which has warped and cracked.1 Leonardo's sfumato ("smoky") technique uses glazes to soften contours and contrasts. King François I, who invited Leonardo to France, bought the painting in 1518, and it now sits in a climate-controlled glass case in the Louvre's largest room, the Salle des États.

Part of its fame comes from a crime. On 21 August 1911 the painting vanished from the Louvre, and nothing was heard of it for over two years, until Vincenzo Peruggia, a glazier who had worked at the Louvre, tried to sell it to an Italian art dealer, who alerted the authorities.2 It came back more famous than ever.

In 1508 Pope Julius II commissioned Michelangelo, already famous for his marble David, to paint the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel in the Vatican. The contract asked for the twelve apostles; Michelangelo instead covered a ceiling about 39 by 13.7 metres, nearly 800 square metres, with scenes from Genesis, prophets and nudes, finishing in 1512. In The Creation of Adam, a powerful God reaches towards a languid Adam, their fingers about to touch across an empty gap. The central panel, though, is the Creation of Eve.

The popular image of Michelangelo lying flat on his back, alone, is a myth. In 1988 the art historian William Wallace concluded that he stood on innovative scaffolding and had help from as many as 13 assistants,3 who ground colours, mixed paints and painted much of the architecture, decoration and secondary figures. Michelangelo described his pose to a friend: "My beard toward Heaven, I feel the back of my brain upon my neck."

title: Baroque to Romanticism: Drama, Militias and Academies
description: Caravaggio's light, Rembrandt's Night Watch, the Academy and its Salon, and Romantic Turner

concepts.title: Caravaggio: Saints From the Street
concepts.contentHtml:
Michelangelo Merisi took the name Caravaggio from his home town in Lombardy. He arrived in Rome in 1592, aged 21, and sold still lifes and half-length figures on the street until Cardinal Francesco del Monte took him into his household in 1595. His first public commissions, the paintings of Saint Matthew in the Contarelli Chapel of San Luigi dei Francesi in Rome, made him a celebrity almost overnight.

See his style in The Supper at Emmaus (1601) in the National Gallery, London. The risen Christ, young and beardless in a red tunic, blesses bread at an inn table. His two disciples, shown as ordinary working men with lined faces and ragged clothes, suddenly recognise him: one is about to leap out of his chair, his elbow jutting towards you, while the other flings out his arms in a pose that recalls the Crucifixion. The innkeeper looks on unmoved, his face in shadow, and a basket of fruit teeters on the edge of the table.

The drama comes from chiaroscuro, strong contrasts of light and shade: a hard light from the left picks out faces and hands against the dark. Caravaggio also broke studio habits. He painted straight onto the canvas with minimal preparation, sometimes scratching lines into the priming to mark where figures went, and not a single drawing that can be firmly attributed to him survives.1 Critics were horrified that he used people with rough, characterful faces as models for saints.

His life was as violent as his light. He was arrested for, among other things, throwing a plate of artichokes at a waiter.2 In 1606 he killed a man in a swordfight and fled Rome for Naples, then Malta, where he became a knight, landed in prison, escaped and was expelled, then Sicily. Friends won him a papal pardon, but he fell ill, perhaps with malaria, and died in 1610. His lighting shaped painters all over Europe.

concepts.title: The Night Watch Is Not at Night
concepts.contentHtml:
In 17th-century Amsterdam, citizens commissioned art too. The city's civic guard companies, its militia and police, ordered group portraits for their halls. In 1642 Rembrandt van Rijn finished the most famous of them for the great hall of the arquebusiers' guild: Militia Company of District II under the Command of Captain Frans Banninck Cocq, better known as The Night Watch. It is 379.5 by 453.5 centimetres, his largest canvas, and it hangs in the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam.1

Earlier militia portraits lined their sitters up neatly. Rembrandt painted a moment in motion. The captain, dressed in black, gestures as he tells his brightly lit lieutenant to start the company marching. Around them guardsmen with pikes and muskets fall into formation, a drummer beats his drum, a dog barks and a gun goes off. In the background a glowing young girl, the company's mascot, catches the light. The Rijksmuseum calls it the first group portrait whose figures are actually doing something.

Now the myth. Despite its dark tones, the scene is a daylight march, not a night watch. The nickname, in use since the end of the 18th century, grew from that misreading. Part of the gloom is varnish, the transparent top coat that protects paint but turns yellow and dull with age.

The painting has had a hard life. When it moved to the Town Hall on Dam Square in 1715, it was physically cut down to fit its new place. In 1975 a visitor slashed it with a bread knife, and it has also survived acid damage. In the project called Operation Night Watch, the Rijksmuseum spent five years researching the canvas before starting to remove the old varnish, working with microscopic precision inside a glass chamber in full view of visitors.

concepts.title: Academies, the Salon and the Romantic Storm
concepts.contentHtml:
Before the Renaissance, painters belonged to guilds and were treated as craftsmen. Academies set out to raise their status and train them, ideally under a royal patron. The most powerful was the French Académie Royale de Peinture et de Sculpture, established in 1648 and housed in the Louvre.1 It began holding exhibitions in 1663 and opened them to the public from 1673; these official shows became known as the Salon. London's Royal Academy followed in 1768, with Joshua Reynolds as its first president.

The academies ranked subjects in a hierarchy of genres. At the top stood history painting, scenes from classical history, mythology and the Bible, in an idealised "grand style". Below came portraits, scenes of daily life (genre painting), landscape and still life.

A Salon hit could make a career. At the Salon of 1834, crowds pressed forward to see Paul Delaroche's The Execution of Lady Jane Grey (1833), about 2.5 by 3 metres, with life-size figures on a stage-like platform. The blindfolded 17-year-old, glowing in white satin, gropes for the block, gently guided by the Lieutenant of the Tower; the executioner waits with his axe, and straw lies ready to soak up the blood. It is not accurate, since the real execution took place outdoors. Then the twist: for decades it was thought to have been destroyed in the Thames flood of 1928, until it was rediscovered by chance in the basement of the Tate Gallery in 1973.2 It now hangs in the National Gallery, London.

Against classical restraint, Romanticism, at its height from about 1780 to 1830, prized emotion, personal feeling and nature. J. M. W. Turner's The Fighting Temeraire (1839, National Gallery) shows a veteran warship of Trafalgar, ghostly in white and gold, towed up the Thames by a black steam tug to be broken up, under a blazing sunset. Turner probably never saw the towing; he recreated it from reports and bent facts for feeling, since a ship heading west up the Thames could not have had the sunset behind it in the east.3

title: The 19th Century: Realism, the Camera and the Refused
description: Courbet's Realism, the first photographs, and the Salon des Refusés of 1863

concepts.title: Courbet: Painting What Is There
concepts.contentHtml:
By the mid-19th century the academies had grown conservative, and the Paris Salon preferred grand scenes from the past. Gustave Courbet wanted the present. At the Salon that opened in 1850 and ran into 1851, he showed two enormous canvases of ordinary people: The Stonebreakers, inspired by two men he saw working along a road, and A Burial at Ornans.

The Burial, painted in 1849–50 and now in the Musée d'Orsay in Paris, shows a funeral in Courbet's home town, Ornans, and real townspeople posed for it. Clergy, a mayor and men and women from all walks of life stand in a long, frieze-like line around a gaping grave strewn with bones, in dark greens and dull greys, with a crucifix rising above them, all arranged without any thought to class distinction. The shock was its size, about 3.15 by 6.68 metres. That was the scale of history painting, reserved for heroes and gods, here given to villagers, life-size and unidealised.1 Traditional critics attacked it; the critic Champfleury, the first to use the word "realism" in art criticism, hailed it as a landmark.

Courbet is often quoted as saying: "Show me an angel and I will paint one." In 1855 Paris held a world's fair, the Exposition Universelle. Eleven of his works were accepted, but the jury rejected two of his most ambitious,2 the Burial and his huge The Painter's Studio. Courbet's answer was new. He had a pavilion built near the exhibition, called it the Pavilion of Realism and hung forty of his paintings in it.3 By staging his own show, he challenged the authority of the official art institutions, and gave Realism a name and a programme: paint the life of your own time, as it is.

concepts.title: 1839: The Camera Arrives
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1839 the invention of photography was announced, simultaneously in France and England, dazzling the public. But the oldest surviving camera photograph is twelve years older. In 1827 Joseph Nicéphore Niépce dissolved light-sensitive bitumen in oil of lavender, coated a polished pewter plate with it, put the plate in a camera obscura and set it near the window of his upstairs workroom at Saint-Loup-de-Varennes in Burgundy. After several days of exposure to sunlight, the plate held an image of the courtyard, outbuildings and trees outside.1 He had been making fleeting camera pictures since 1816, and he called his process héliographie, "sun writing".

That plate, View from the Window at Le Gras, measures just 16.7 by 20.3 centimetres. It passed through private hands in Britain before it was bought by the Harry Ransom Center at the University of Texas at Austin in 1963.2 Niépce himself called his method "the first uncertain step in a completely new direction". Think about that: the first surviving camera photograph took not a click but days.

In 1829 Niépce went into partnership with Louis-Jacques-Mandé Daguerre, who ran the famous Diorama in Paris, where paintings were shown in a rotating auditorium with spectacular light effects. After Niépce died, Daguerre kept improving the process and introduced the daguerreotype in 1839. Painting and the new optical spectacles were already entangled: the National Gallery thinks Delaroche, composing Lady Jane Grey, was almost certainly aware of panoramas and dioramas. And in the very year the daguerreotype was announced, Turner exhibited The Fighting Temeraire at the Royal Academy.

Did the camera kill painting? Not then. In 1863 the Salon jury was faced with some 5,000 works. But painters now shared the world with a machine that could record what was in front of it, and the question of what painting could do that a camera could not runs through the Modern Art topic.

concepts.title: 1863: The Salon of the Refused
concepts.contentHtml:
By the 1860s the Salon jury held real power: patrons often would not buy a work the jury had refused. In 1863 it rejected more than half of the roughly 5,000 works presented, and the uproar was so loud that Emperor Napoleon III ordered an exhibition of the refused works to open next to the official Salon, so the public could judge for itself. The Salon des Refusés opened on 15 May 1863, a few feet from the official show. More than 600 artists withdrew, afraid of hanging beside inferior work and of reprisals from future juries, but as many as four thousand visitors came on Sundays, when admission was free.1

The star of the scandal was Édouard Manet's Le Déjeuner sur l'herbe (Luncheon on the Grass), shown under the title Le Bain, 208 by 264.5 centimetres and now in the Musée d'Orsay. A naked woman sits at a woodland picnic between two men in contemporary clothes and looks straight out at you, beside an overturned basket of fruit. Manet borrowed the theme from the Pastoral Concert, now in the Louvre, but his figures were neither allegorical nor mythological; they were plainly contemporary. Critics attacked his drawing, composition and handling of paint even more than the subject.2

The problem was not nudity. At the official Salon that same year, Alexandre Cabanel's The Birth of Venus, a voluptuous goddess emerging from the waves in an inviting pose, was received in triumph, and Napoleon III bought it himself.3 A goddess was acceptable; a real body in a modern setting broke the academic rules. Émile Zola mocked Cabanel's goddess as made of "a sort of pink and white marzipan".

The Salon never fully recovered its authority. Younger artists grew determined to hold jury-free exhibitions and adopted Manet as their unofficial leader, even though he sought the Salon's approval all his life and never showed with the Impressionists. Many regard 1863 as a turning point in modern art, and the Modern Art topic picks up the story with Impressionism.

title: After 1900, and Who Tells the Story
description: Cubism, abstraction and the readymade, how art historians know, and who was left out

concepts.title: After 1900: The Rules Break Fast
concepts.contentHtml:
From here the pace quickens, and the Modern Art topic takes you through it in depth. Three breaks are worth knowing now.

Cubism was invented around 1907–08 by Pablo Picasso and Georges Braque, and is generally agreed to begin with Picasso's Les Demoiselles d'Avignon (1907). By breaking figures and objects into planes, the artists showed different viewpoints at the same time, abandoning the single fixed viewpoint of linear perspective that had ruled since the Renaissance. Picasso, inspired partly by African masks, put it bluntly: "A head is a matter of eyes, nose, mouth, which can be distributed in any way you like." The name came from the critic Louis Vauxcelles, who in 1908 said Braque's paintings reduced everything to "geometric outlines, to cubes".1

Abstraction holds a surprise. Kandinsky, Malevich and Mondrian are usually named as its pioneers, but the Swedish artist Hilma af Klint began radically abstract paintings in 1906, years before them.2 Her Paintings for the Temple (1906–1915) grew from spiritualism and Theosophy and were made partly through her practice as a medium. She rarely exhibited them and stipulated that they not be shown for twenty years after her death. The Guggenheim in New York gave them a major exhibition in 2018–19.

Then came the most radical move of all. In 1917 in New York, Marcel Duchamp took a men's urinal, signed it with a false name and exhibited it placed on its back.3 He called it Fountain (Tate in London owns a 1964 replica), one of his readymades, ordinary manufactured objects chosen out of "visual indifference". An editorial in a magazine he ran with two friends, The Blind Man, said it did not matter whether Mr Mutt had made it himself: "He CHOSE it." The artist as chooser rather than maker opened the way to conceptual art, and whether such a thing is art at all is the question the Modern Art topic takes on.

concepts.title: How Do Art Historians Know?
concepts.contentHtml:
Throughout this topic you have met claims about who made what, when and why. Art historians build them from three kinds of evidence, and each has limits.

Documents. Inventories, contracts, letters and trial records pin works down. The Arnolfini Portrait can be traced to 17 July 1516, when an inventory of Margaret of Austria's paintings listed1 "a large picture which is called Hernoul le Fin with his wife in a chamber", done "by the painter Johannes". From her it passed into the Spanish royal collection, then to a Scottish soldier, James Hay, and in 1842 to the National Gallery.

The trained eye. Connoisseurship means judging authorship by style and quality, and it can deadlock. Giotto often relied on assistants and signed work they had helped to make. The frescoes of the life of Saint Francis in the Upper Basilica at Assisi may have been supervised by him without being painted by him, and the debate still rages.2 Old writers need the same care. Giorgio Vasari tells how the painter Cimabue met a shepherd boy of about ten scratching a picture of a sheep on a stone with another stone, and took him on: the boy was Giotto.3 It is a lovely anecdote, written by a man born more than two centuries after Giotto, and the same Vasari gave the Gothic style its insulting name. Treat such stories as stories until documents back them.

The laboratory. Science now answers many questions of what and when: uranium-thorium dating for cave paint, micro-CT for the Willendorf stone, ultraviolet and raking light for Greek colour, infrared reflectography for van Eyck's underdrawing, synchrotron analysis for the oil at Bamiyan. The Forgeries topic shows the same tools catching fakes. Science is weaker on who and why, and the strongest conclusions come when all three kinds of evidence agree.

concepts.title: Who Gets Into the Story?
concepts.contentHtml:
In January 1971 the art historian Linda Nochlin published an essay in ARTnews with a deliberately awkward title: "Why Have There Been No Great Women Artists?" Her answer turned the question round. The fault, she wrote, "lies not in our stars, our hormones, our menstrual cycles or our empty internal spaces, but in our institutions and our education". She mocked the myth of the Great Artist born with a "golden nugget" of genius, and gave a concrete case: for long periods women art students were denied any access to nude models, a basic part of an artist's training.1

Consider Artemisia Gentileschi (1593 to 1654 or later), whom the National Gallery calls the most celebrated female painter of the 17th century. Trained by her father, Orazio, she was raped at 17 by the painter Agostino Tassi; at the trial in 1612, whose records survive, she testified and was tortured. Tassi was found guilty and banished from Rome, though the sentence was never enforced. In Florence she became an early woman member of the Academy of the Arts of Drawing in 1616.2 Her Self Portrait as Saint Catherine of Alexandria (about 1615–17) is about 70 centimetres square and shows her life-size, in a turban, gazing straight at you as she leans on the spiked, broken wheel of the saint's torture, a martyr's palm held between thumb and forefinger. The strong side light owes much to Caravaggio. Wait, really? The picture was only discovered in 2017, and the National Gallery bought it soon afterwards.3

Like Caravaggio, Artemisia was admired in her lifetime and then forgotten, and her work has been properly re-evaluated only in the last 50 years. Activists keep counting. In 1989 the Guerrilla Girls went to the Metropolitan Museum of Art to count women artists on show against naked female bodies in the artworks,4 and made the result a poster: "Do Women Have to Be Naked to Get Into the Met. Museum?" They have recounted since, most recently in 2025. Rewriting the canon also means looking beyond Europe, which is the subject of the Art Beyond Europe topic.
